newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: BP sees rich deep water African oil prospects.
newsitem.headline: BP sees rich deep water African oil prospects.

text.p: Deep water around western and southern Africa offers significant oil production and revenue opportunities, extending well into the next century, British Petroleum Co Plc said on Thursday.

"The possibility that we have in mind is that future production opportunities lie off Africa in the deeper water," David Bamford, head of BP's sub-Saharan Business Unit said at the Africa Upstream 1996 conference.
But he said that the key to developing these resources was improving the relationship between major oil companies and national oil companies (NOCs).
"The single most important thing to delivering that is the quality of the relationship between major oil companies like ourselves and the NOCs. This is the key, the heart," he said.

Sub-Saharan Africa in particular offered significant deep water oil production possibilities, which were achievable but by no means certain, and whose development lay with the application of advanced technology, Bamford said.
Deep water zones were those lying between 200 metres and 2,000 metres and were provinces which contained billions of barrels of oil and several giant fields.
He cited world examples as being the Campos Basin offshore Brazil -- a direct analogue of what might exist offshore sub-Saharan Africa -- and the Mississipi Canyon area of the Gulf of Mexico.
Bamford said development of such resources should aim for production four years after discovery and therefore the industry should find ways to speed up the execution of the risky exploration period.

"I predict that there is need for little other than incremental progress to deliver developments out to 2,000 metres water depth...out to 1,500 metres most milestones have been achieved or are achievable, though not inexpensively.

"From 1,500 metres to 2,000 metres some innovations are required and costs will certainly go up sharply. However, this should not be seen as a barrier but considered simply a question of striking the right risk-reward balance," he said.
Bamford added that geophysics and drilling technology was advancing at a rapid pace and so allowed talk of exploiting resources at vast depths beneath the sea.

Major oil companies had a "pretty poor profile" with regard to world exploration and development -- indulging in selective truth telling and treating the people of countries they operated in carelessly, Bamford said.
"We in BP believe the key to progress in our industry is to seek relationships, activities and projects that have at their heart the mutual advantage of all sides," he said.
